reconcile.connective: Gill treats Matthew and Levi as one man under two names, the apostle preferring the name by which he was best known.

discrepancy.connective: D. F. Strauss presses the objection: the apostle-lists give other disciples' surnames but never call Matthew 'Levi,' undermining the two-names harmonization.

skeptic.name: D. F. Strauss
skeptic.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined
skeptic.attribution: D. F. Strauss (d. 1874), The Life of Jesus Critically Examined (1846)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The other evangelists call him Levi, who was the son of Alphaeus: he went by two names; Mark and Luke call him by the name, which perhaps was the more honourable, or the least known, on purpose to conceal the former life of the apostle, which might expose him to the contempt of some; but he himself chooses to mention the name by which he was most known, as an apostle, and that the grace of God might appear the more illustrious in his calling and conversion.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly explains why Matthew 9:9 names him 'Matthew' while Mark 2:14/Luke 5:27 name him 'Levi' for the same call scene, offering a rationale (self-effacement of the former reputation) for the dual name.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Matthew 9:8
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this exact naming difference, arguing Matthew and Levi are one man under two names. (John Haley's Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible was checked directly via full-text search for 'Levi', 'publican', and the Matt 9:9/Mark 2:14 citation forms and does not treat this passage at all, so Gill is used per the contract's fallback clause.)
